transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I... I suppose I'm here because my family thought it would be a good idea, but honestly, it’s really because of this... this entire situation that’s been going on for months now. I manage an office, you see, I supervise a whole administrative support team, so I know exactly how schedules and paperwork are supposed to be handled. I know what a simple clerical error looks like. 

But what's been happening lately is absolutely not just a series of random mistakes. I've been seeing the exact same pattern, over and over again. My sister’s appointments suddenly get moved without anyone notifying me, and then the bills show up completely wrong, and when I try to get to the bottom of it, people conveniently "forget" to call me back. I'll leave three detailed voicemails with the front desk, and nothing. 

Everyone—the staff, my own family—they all just wave it off and say, "Oh, it's just an oversight, people are busy, it's just a mistake." But you don't have that many "mistakes" in a row. It's statistically impossible. I know what they're doing. They are deliberately keeping information from me. They're trying to push me out of making decisions, trying to cut me out of the loop completely so they can do whatever they want behind my back. It's incredibly frustrating, because I have everything documented, every single phone call and date, and they still act like I'm the one making a fuss over nothing.
Aside from these experiences with your family and the office staff, have you been hearing, seeing, or sensing things that others around you do not seem to notice?

Hearing or seeing things? Like... like voices or visions? No, absolutely not. I want to be very clear about that, Dr. Smith. I am a very grounded person. You don't get to manage an administrative team for as long as I have by imagining things. I deal in facts. Spreadsheets, timecards, concrete data. 

Now, do I notice things that other people miss? Yes, of course I do, but that's because I'm trained to pay attention to details, not because my mind is playing tricks on me. For example, I notice when an email gets CC'd to someone who has absolutely no business being on that thread. Or... or the way the receptionist shifted her weight and looked at the floor when I asked her about the missing paperwork last Tuesday. Most people wouldn't catch that. They’re too wrapped up in their own little worlds, or they just don't care enough to look closely. But I see the real things happening right in front of me. 

So if my family sent me here hoping I'd tell you I'm seeing ghosts or hearing voices from the television, well, that's just another tactic to discredit me. It really is. They want everyone to think I'm losing my grip so no one will look at the actual, physical proof I have. Because I do have it, you know. I brought a whole folder showing exactly how the appointment dates were altered, and I can walk you through it line by line if you want to see what I'm actually looking at. But no, I am not seeing things that aren't there. I'm just seeing the things they wish I wouldn't.
When you are at work or talking with your family, have people ever told you that your thoughts seem to jump around or that they have a hard time following the logic of what you are saying?

No, no one has ever said that to me. In fact, it’s quite the opposite. People are always telling me how organized I am, how I always have everything laid out so perfectly. You know, when you manage an office, you have to be logical. Everything has to follow a sequence. First this happens, then this happens, and if step B doesn't happen, you have to go back and figure out why step A failed. So my thoughts don't "jump around." I am extremely methodical. 

Now, do people sometimes have a hard time following what I'm saying? Well... yes, but not because my logic is flawed. It's because they aren't keeping up. Like my brother, for instance. I sat down with him last weekend—it was Sunday, right after lunch, around 1:30—and I tried to explain to him how the billing cycles at the clinic overlap with the dates my sister's appointments were mysteriously changed. I had my folder, I had the dates highlighted in yellow, the discrepancies in pink. I was walking him through it, step by step, showing him the timeline. And he just sighed, rubbed his eyes, and said, "I can't follow all this, you're making my head spin." 

But that's not my thoughts jumping around, Dr. Smith. That's him refusing to engage with the facts. He didn't want to follow the logic because if he followed the logic, he would have to admit that I'm right. He would have to admit that there is a deliberate pattern here. It's much easier for them to just say, "Oh, you're talking too fast," or "You're overcomplicating things," than to actually look at the spreadsheet I created. I even color-coded it so a child could understand it! But no, my mind is perfectly clear. It’s their willingness to listen that’s the problem.

Do you believe that these patterns of interference are limited to your family and your specific office, or do you feel that this is part of a larger, more organized effort involving other people or groups outside of those circles?

Well, that's an interesting question, Dr. Smith. A very interesting question. Because you see, when I first started noticing the discrepancies—and this was back in early October, right around the time the clinic switched to that new scheduling software, which I know all about because my office uses a similar system—when I first noticed it, I thought it was just the front desk staff being incompetent. I really did. I thought, "Okay, they're poorly trained, they don't understand how to merge files, they're just making a mess of my sister's records." And my family, of course, they just went along with whatever the clinic told them, because they don't want to rock the boat. 

But then... then I started looking at the timestamps on the emails. And the IP addresses. I mean, I'm not an IT expert, but I know enough to look at the headers, and I noticed that some of these changes were being made after hours. Who is logging into a clinic scheduling system at 11:45 on a Friday night to move a routine follow-up appointment? It didn't make any sense. And that's when I realized, it's not just the receptionist. It can't be. The receptionist doesn't have the authority or the access to bypass the system's audit logs. I know this for a fact because I set up the permissions for my own administrative team, and you don't just give a front desk clerk override privileges. 

So, to answer your question, no, I don't think it's just my family and a few lazy office workers. It's too coordinated. It's too precise. Someone higher up has to be involved. I'm not saying it's the government or the CIA or something ridiculous like that—I'm a practical woman, Dr. Smith, I don't believe in spy movies. But I do believe in corporate mismanagement, and I believe there are people, perhaps the clinic administrators, perhaps someone at the insurance company, who are deliberately manipulating these records. Why? I don't know yet. Maybe it's a billing fraud scheme and they're using my sister's account to hide it. Maybe they realized I was catching on to their little game and now they're actively trying to shut me out so I don't expose them. 

I actually started a separate binder just for the insurance EOBs—the Explanation of Benefits forms—because if you line them up with the altered appointment dates, you can see a very clear pattern of upcoding. I brought that binder too, if you want to see it. It's the blue one in my tote bag. I spent all of last weekend cross-referencing the procedure codes, and I can tell you right now, there is absolutely no way this is limited to just a few people making mistakes. It's systemic. It has to be.
Aside from your work and the situation with your family, have you found that you have less interest in hobbies, socializing, or taking care of your usual daily responsibilities lately?

Less interest? No. No, absolutely not. Let me stop you right there, Dr. Smith, because I know exactly what that question implies. You're asking if I'm... what, neglecting myself? Letting the house go? Sitting around in a bathrobe staring at the wall? No. Not even close. 

Outside of dealing with my sister’s appointments and, you know, trying to get straight answers from these people—which, as I've explained, is practically a part-time job in itself because of all the runaround they give me—I am functioning perfectly. Better than perfectly, actually. I still keep my home in immaculate order. I vacuum twice a week, I do my laundry on a strict schedule, I meal prep on Sundays... I mean, just yesterday I reorganized the pantry because the canned goods weren't facing label-out. 

And my finances? Please. I pay all my bills on time, usually a week early. I sit down every Friday evening at my desk, I open my online banking, and I reconcile every single penny. I don't miss payments. And of course, I still do my job. I show up every day, I manage my staff, I run the payroll, I handle the vendor contracts... I haven't missed a single beat at work. 

So, yes, I know my brother and the rest of them might tell you that I spend too much time on the computer, or they might think I’m too focused on this whole situation with the clinic and the insurance records. They see my binders and they think, "Oh, she's obsessed." But just because I am dedicated to uncovering the truth doesn't mean my life is falling apart. I am absolutely not falling apart, and I am certainly not acting strangely in other parts of my life. I am exactly the same organized, responsible woman I have always been. It takes a lot of energy to keep a household running and manage an office while also conducting a thorough investigation, but I assure you, I am more than capable of handling my daily responsibilities.
